t.3.78.1: Bṛhadaśva said: When the city had grown calm and joyful, and a great festival had begun, the king brought Damayantī home with a large army.
t.3.78.2: Damayantī too was honored by her father, Bhīma of immeasurable spirit and terrible prowess, slayer of enemy heroes, who then sent her forth.
t.3.78.3: But when Vaidarbhī had come back together with her children, King Nala lived on joyfully, like the king of the gods in the Nandana grove.
t.3.78.4: Thus he attained renown among the kings of Jambūdvīpa; and the greatly glorious one, having won back his kingdom, dwelt once more in his own realm.
t.3.78.6: Through gambling, O best of men, O bull of the Bharatas, Nala, conqueror of enemy cities, together with his wife, met with such suffering.
t.3.78.5: And he sacrificed according to rule with sacrifices of many kinds, accompanied by ample sacrificial fees. In the same way you too, lord of kings, together with your friends, will soon be spoken of.
t.3.78.7: O lord of the earth, Nala, all alone, met with very great and terrible suffering, and yet he attained prosperity again.
t.3.78.8: But you, Pāṇḍava, accompanied by your brothers and by Kṛṣṇā, take your delight in this great forest, reflecting on dharma alone.
t.3.78.9: And you are constantly attended, O king, by illustrious brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; why then this lamenting?
t.3.78.10: This tale, too, is said to destroy Kali; having heard it, O lord of the people, one such as you can take comfort.
t.3.78.11: Reflecting always on the instability of human wealth, both in its gain and in its loss, take comfort and do not grieve.
t.3.78.12: Those who will narrate this great story of Nala, and those who will hear it again and again, misfortune will never attend them. Riches will come to such a one, and he will attain prosperity.
t.3.78.13: Having heard this ancient and ever-excellent history, a man will obtain sons, grandsons and cattle, and pre-eminence among men; he will be free from disease and full of joy, there is no doubt.
t.3.78.14: And the fear that you see, thinking, “A man skilled at dice will challenge me again,” that fear of yours I shall destroy, O king.
t.3.78.16: Then the king, delighted at heart, said to Bṛhadaśva: "Blessed one, I wish to know the secret of the dice in its true essence."
t.3.78.15: I know the entire secret of the dice, O you whose prowess is true. Receive it, Kaunteya; being pleased, I tell it to you.
t.3.78.17: Then he gave the secret of the dice to the great-souled Pāṇḍava; and having also given him the lore called the Horse's Head, the great ascetic went away to perform his ablutions.
t.3.78.18: When Bṛhadaśva had gone, he heard that Pārtha Savyasācin, the wise one, was engaged in fierce austerity, living on air alone.
t.3.78.19: To the brahmins and ascetics who came flocking from here and there, and to those who had gathered from the finest sacred fords and mountains, he of firm vows...
t.3.78.21: How Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Pṛthā, an ascetic firm in his vows, a solitary sage, glorious, is like Dharma embodied.
t.3.78.20: Thus the mighty-armed Pārtha has undertaken an austerity hard to achieve, and no one else of such fierce austerity has ever been seen before.
t.3.78.22: Hearing that he was practicing austerities in the great forest, O king, the Pāṇḍava, son of Kuntī, grieved for his dear brother Jaya.
t.3.78.23: But Yudhiṣṭhira, with a burning heart, seeking refuge in the great forest, questioned the Brahmins of manifold knowledge.
